leadBefore: How long an assertion issued here is valid for, and how far its window is widened at each end to allow for a relying party whose clock disagrees with this one. All three are
leadMiddle: : the two lifetimes are also drawn on
leadAfter: , one on each, and the skew on both. This page is a shorter way to the same rows and the only place all three are visible at once — it writes through the same function, so a change made here and one made there are one change.
nextOnly: A change applies to the NEXT assertion and to nothing already issued. A validity window is stamped into an assertion as Conditions/NotBefore and NotOnOrAfter when it is signed, so an assertion already in a relying party’s hands cannot be shortened or extended afterwards by anything on this page.
defaultsBefore: Ten of these eleven are DEFAULTS, not decisions. Each is what an application gets when its own entry says nothing, and the Per-application column names the attribute that overrides it — set that on an application under
defaultsAfter: and this row stops governing it. The eleventh, the clock skew, has no per-application form: it is a fact about the clocks in the estate this service issues into, decided once. They moved here from the two identity provider pages on 2026-08-27, because those pages configure this service as an identity provider and these describe what it does for an application nobody has configured.
units: The two lifetimes are in minutes and the skew and the two artifact lifetimes are in seconds, which is not a formatting accident: a lifetime is set to a number of minutes to watch an assertion go stale, and a skew is a handful of seconds covering the difference between two machines. The skew is capped at 300 seconds for the reason oauth2.clockSkewS is — five minutes is what Kerberos allows here (krb5.clockSkew), and wider than that the window has stopped being a tolerance and become a lifetime nobody chose.
allChecked: All sixteen are checked before any is applied — a form that took eleven and refused the twelfth would leave this service issuing a combination nobody chose.
overriddenCount: {n} of the sixteen are set here, {kept}.
putBackNote: It clears the override on these sixteen only, and leaves any other setting alone —
noneOverridden: None of the sixteen is overridden: each is coming from its environment variable, from {file}, or from {defaults} under it. The Source column says which.
hSkew: What the skew actually does to an assertion
skewBothEnds: It is added at BOTH ends of the window and to neither instant that states when something happened: NotBefore is backdated by it and NotOnOrAfter is extended by it, while IssueInstant and the authentication instant are left at the real time — backdating those would be a lie about an event rather than an allowance about a clock. So the window an assertion states is its lifetime plus twice the skew, which is why this page reports saml2WindowS and saml11WindowS beside the settings themselves. At the default 0 the documents are byte-for-byte what this service issued before the setting existed.
hFour: It reaches four protocols, and it is not the skew this service reads with
four: Four. WS-Trust and WS-Federation build their assertions with the same two functions the browser profiles use, so both settings above reach them without either module knowing these exist. A WS-Federation sign-in carries a SAML 1.1 assertion, so it is saml11.assertionLifetimeMin that governs it. What those two wrap the assertion in — WS-Trust’s wsu:Lifetime and the equivalent in a WS-Federation response — states the LIFETIME without the skew, which is the conservative reading and is deliberate: the envelope describes what was asked for and the assertion states what it is actually valid for.
notOauthBefore: And it is not oauth2.clockSkewS. That one is the allowance applied wherever this service READS something back — including an inbound federation partner’s SAML assertion at {path}, which applies it to exactly the two attributes this page writes. This one is what goes INTO a document this service issues. One is about somebody else’s clock and one is about how much of somebody else’s clock this service pays for in advance, and a deployment wanting a strict reading and a forgiving issuance has to be able to say so. The reading tolerance is on
outThere: Counted against this service’s own clock with no allowance applied — the skew above is written into an assertion rather than applied when one is read here, so an assertion this calls expired is one whose stated NotOnOrAfter has passed. {held} artifact(s) are held, of the most recent {cap}; {forgotten} older one(s) have been forgotten. Every one of them is on
outThereAfter: , which draws assertions beside the JWTs and the Kerberos tickets.
hTwoThings: Two things about a window this page does not set
twoThings: A SAML artifact is good for saml2.artifactTtlS and is a different clock entirely — it governs how long an artifact can be RESOLVED for, not how long the assertion it resolves to is valid. And the session behind an assertion has its own lifetime: an assertion that has expired does not end the sign-on session that produced it, which is why a relying party refusing a stale assertion can be sent straight back here and get a fresh one with no sign-in screen.
footer: The same three over JSON are at /admin/saml-assertions?format=json and GET /admin-api/saml-assertions; the two actions on this page are POST /admin-api/saml-assertions/set and /defaults. They are also three ordinary rows of GET /admin-api/config.
warnSkewLong: The clock skew is at least as long as the {kind} assertion’s own lifetime ({skew} against {lifetime}). The window written into the assertion is the lifetime plus the skew at EACH end, so it is valid for at least three times as long as {key} says. If the point was to watch a relying party refuse a stale assertion, it will not: lower the skew, or raise the lifetime.
warnSkewZero: The skew is 0, which is what this service has always done — NotBefore is stamped at exactly the moment of issue. That is the strict reading, and it is the one that fails against a relying party whose clock is a few seconds behind: the assertion is not yet valid when it arrives, and the refusal reads as a signature or trust-store problem from both ends. If a service provider is refusing assertions that look correct, this is the first setting to raise.
